chapters.n: Paul writes a second surviving letter to Corinth, this time with Timothy, addressing the saints in Corinth and throughout Achaia (southern Greece). It is his most personal letter.

f.g: The Roman province of southern Greece, with Corinth as its capital.

chapters.n: His usual greeting: grace and peace from the Father and the Son.

f.w: Grace be to you and peace

chapters.n: Paul bursts into praise of God, the Father of Jesus Christ, whom he calls the source of all mercy and comfort.
God comforts us in every trouble so that we can comfort others with the same comfort we received. Our trials can equip us to help others.

f.w: comfort them which are in any trouble

chapters.n: As the apostles share abundantly in Christ’s sufferings, they also receive abundant comfort through Him.

f.w: the sufferings of Christ abound in us

chapters.n: Whether Paul suffers or is comforted, it all works for the Corinthians’ good, helping them endure the same kind of trials patiently.
Paul’s hope for them is firm: as they share in sufferings, they will also share in comfort.
Paul describes a crushing ordeal in the province of Asia — so severe he thought he would die.

f.w: our trouble which came to us in Asia
f.g: Perhaps the riot at Ephesus or another unrecorded danger.

chapters.n: He felt he had received a death sentence. This taught him not to rely on himself but on God, who raises the dead.
God rescued him from deadly peril, still rescues him, and Paul trusts He will keep doing so.
The saints’ prayers helped. Many prayed, so many will give thanks for God’s blessing on Paul.
Paul’s confidence is a clear conscience: he has lived honestly and sincerely, not with worldly cunning, but by God’s grace — especially toward them.
His letters mean exactly what they say, with no hidden agenda. He hopes they will fully understand him.
They already partly understand that they can be proud of Paul, as he will be of them at Christ’s coming.

f.w: the day of the Lord Jesus

chapters.n: Paul had originally planned to visit them twice, giving them a double blessing.

f.g: A second blessing or favor from two visits.

chapters.n: His plan was Corinth, then Macedonia, then back to Corinth, then on to Judea with their help.
When he changed his plans, some accused him of being fickle — saying yes and no at the same time. Paul asks if that is fair.
As surely as God is faithful, Paul’s word to them has not been unreliable.

f.g: A solemn oath: God is faithful.

chapters.n: The Christ whom Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy preached isn’t wishy-washy; in Him God’s answer is always “yes.”
Every promise God has made is fulfilled in Christ. That is why we say “Amen” through Him, to God’s glory.

f.g: Amen = “so it is” — Christ guarantees God’s promises.

chapters.n: God is the one who makes them firm in Christ and has anointed them.

f.g: Set apart with the Spirit, as kings and priests were anointed with oil.

chapters.n: God has put His seal of ownership on them and given the Spirit as a down payment on what is to come.

f.g: A down payment guaranteeing full payment later.

chapters.n: Paul calls God as witness: he delayed his visit to spare them a painful, disciplinary encounter.
Apostles don’t dictate people’s faith; they work alongside them for their joy. Their faith is their own, and by it they stand firm.
Paul decided not to make another painful visit. Many think he had already made a sorrowful trip to Corinth after writing 1 Corinthians.
If Paul causes them grief, who will cheer him up? Only the very people he made sad. Their relationship is tightly bound.

f.g: Their joy and his are linked.

chapters.n: That’s why he wrote instead of coming — so his visit wouldn’t be full of sorrow, trusting his joy would be theirs too.

f.w: I wrote this same unto you
f.g: Probably a severe letter written between 1 and 2 Corinthians that has not survived.

chapters.n: He wrote that letter in deep anguish and with many tears — not to hurt them but to show how much he loves them.

f.w: the love which I have more abundantly unto you

chapters.n: A particular offender had caused grief to the whole congregation, not just to Paul. Paul is careful not to overstate it.
The discipline the majority imposed on this man is enough.

f.g: Decided by the majority of the congregation.

chapters.n: Now they should forgive and comfort him, so he isn’t overwhelmed by excessive sorrow and despair. Discipline should lead to healing.
Paul urges them to formally reaffirm their love for him and welcome him back.
Paul wrote partly to test whether they would follow apostolic counsel in everything.
Whomever they forgive, Paul forgives too, acting in Christ’s presence for their sake.

f.g: In Christ’s presence, as His representative.

chapters.n: Unforgiveness gives Satan an opening. The saints know his schemes to divide and destroy.
Paul recounts that when he arrived at Troas to preach, the Lord opened a door for missionary success.

f.g: A seaport in northwest Asia Minor.

chapters.n: But he was restless because Titus, bringing news from Corinth, hadn’t arrived. So he left for Macedonia to find him.

f.g: A Gentile convert and trusted companion who carried messages to Corinth.

chapters.n: Paul pictures a Roman victory parade, with Christ as the conquering general leading His followers. Like incense in such a parade, the knowledge of Christ spreads everywhere through them.

f.g: A Roman triumph: a victory procession through the city, often with burning incense.

chapters.n: Their lives are a sweet fragrance of Christ offered to God, noticed by those being saved and by those who are perishing.
To those rejecting the gospel, the message smells of death; to those accepting it, it smells of life. Who could be adequate for such a task?

f.w: who is sufficient for these things?

chapters.n: Unlike others who peddle God’s word for profit, Paul speaks sincerely, as sent from God and in His presence.

f.g: Peddle or water it down, like a dishonest merchant diluting wine.

chapters.n: Is Paul bragging again? Does he need letters of recommendation like some visiting teachers? The rival teachers apparently carried such credentials.

f.g: Letters of introduction vouching for a traveler.

chapters.n: The Corinthians themselves are Paul’s letter of recommendation — written on his heart and visible to everyone.
They are a letter from Christ, delivered by Paul, written by the Spirit not with ink, and not on stone tablets like the law of Moses but on human hearts.
Paul has this confidence before God through Christ.
Not that he is competent on his own; his adequacy comes from God.
God made them able servants of a new covenant — not a code of written rules that condemns, but the Spirit that gives life.

f.w: the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life

chapters.n: Even the law of Moses, which brought condemnation, came with such glory that Israel couldn’t look at Moses’ shining face — a glory that faded.

f.g: The law, which revealed sin and its penalty.

chapters.n: How much more glorious, then, is the ministry of the Spirit!
If the ministry that condemned had glory, the ministry that brings righteousness overflows with far more.
Compared to the new covenant’s surpassing glory, the old seems to have no glory at all — like a lamp in the noonday sun.

f.g: The surpassing glory of the gospel.

chapters.n: If what was temporary had glory, what is permanent has much more.
With such hope, the apostles speak with great boldness and openness.
Unlike Moses, who veiled his face so Israel wouldn’t see the glory fade, Paul has nothing to hide.

f.w: put a veil over his face

chapters.n: But Israel’s minds were hardened, and a “veil” still lies over them when the old covenant is read. Only in Christ is that veil removed.

f.g: Old covenant — the scriptures of Moses.

chapters.n: To this day, when Moses is read, a veil covers their hearts.

f.w: the veil is upon their heart
f.g: A spiritual barrier preventing them from seeing Christ in their own scriptures.

chapters.n: But whenever someone turns to the Lord, the veil is lifted — just as Moses removed his veil when he went in to speak with the Lord.

f.w: the veil shall be taken away

chapters.n: The Lord works through the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.
With unveiled faces, believers reflect the Lord’s glory like mirrors and are gradually transformed into His image, from one degree of glory to another, by the Spirit.
Because God mercifully gave them this ministry of the new covenant, the apostles don’t lose heart.

f.g: We don’t give up or lose courage.

chapters.n: They reject secret, shameful tactics and never twist God’s word. Instead they openly declare the truth and let every conscience judge them before God.

f.w: handling the word of God deceitfully

chapters.n: If the gospel seems hidden, it is hidden only from those who are perishing.

f.w: hid to them that are lost

chapters.n: Satan — “the god of this world” — has blinded unbelievers so they can’t see the light of the gospel of Christ, who perfectly shows us what God is like.

f.g: Satan, the false ruler of this fallen age.

chapters.n: The apostles preach Christ as Lord, not themselves; they present themselves as the saints’ servants for Jesus’ sake.
The God who said “Let there be light” at creation has shone into their hearts, revealing His glory in the face of Jesus Christ.

f.w: commanded the light to shine out of darkness
in the face of Jesus Christ

chapters.n: This treasure is held in fragile clay jars — ordinary, weak mortals — so it is clear the extraordinary power comes from God.

f.g: Cheap clay pots, used in that era to store valuables.

chapters.n: Pressed from every side, but not crushed; confused, but not hopeless.

f.g: At a loss, but not utterly at a loss — a wordplay in Greek.

chapters.n: Hunted, but never abandoned by God; knocked down, but not knocked out.
They carry Jesus’ dying in their bodies through constant danger and suffering, so that His life is also displayed in them.

f.w: the dying of the Lord Jesus

chapters.n: They are always being handed over to death for Jesus, so His life can be shown in their mortal bodies.
Their suffering brings spiritual life to the Corinthians.

f.w: death worketh in us, but life in you
f.g: The apostles’ sacrifices produce life in those they serve.

chapters.n: Like the psalmist who said, “I believed, therefore I spoke,” they have that same faith, so they speak.

f.w: I believed, and therefore have I spoken

chapters.n: They know God, who raised Jesus, will raise them too and present them together with the Corinthians.
Everything is for the saints’ benefit, so that as grace reaches more people, thanksgiving multiplies to God’s glory.
So they don’t lose heart. Though their bodies are wearing out, their inner selves are renewed every day.

f.w: the inward man is renewed day by day

chapters.n: Present troubles are light and brief compared with the overwhelming, eternal glory they are preparing.

f.w: light affliction, which is but for a moment

f.g: In Hebrew, “glory” (kavod) also suggests weight or heaviness — a nice contrast with “light” affliction.

chapters.n: So they focus not on what is seen but on the unseen. The visible is temporary; the unseen is eternal.

f.g: Temporary, lasting only for a time.

chapters.n: Paul compares the mortal body to a tent. If it is taken down at death, we have an eternal, God-made dwelling awaiting us — the resurrected body.

f.g: A tent — a temporary dwelling (Paul was a tentmaker).

f.w: an house not made with hands

chapters.n: Meanwhile we groan, longing to be clothed with our heavenly dwelling.
Once clothed with it, we won’t be found “naked” — without a body.

f.g: Disembodied — a spirit without its body.

chapters.n: We groan under burdens in this tent — not wanting to lose a body, but to be clothed with a better one, so that mortality is swallowed up by life.

f.w: mortality might be swallowed up of life

chapters.n: God prepared us for exactly this and gave the Spirit as a guarantee.

f.g: A down payment ensuring full payment.

chapters.n: So we are confident, knowing that as long as we are in this body, we are away from the Lord’s presence.
We live by faith, not by what we can see.

f.w: we walk by faith, not by sight

chapters.n: Paul would rather leave the body and be at home with the Lord.
So, whether here or there, his goal is to please the Lord.
Everyone will stand before Christ’s judgment seat to receive what is due for what was done in mortality, good or bad.

f.w: according to that he hath done

chapters.n: Knowing the fear of the Lord, they try to persuade people. God knows their hearts, and Paul hopes the Corinthians do too.

f.g: Reverent fear of the Lord as Judge.

chapters.n: Paul isn’t praising himself; he’s giving the saints a reason to be proud of him, so they can answer critics who value outward show over the heart.

f.w: glory in appearance, and not in heart

chapters.n: If they seem out of their minds, it is for God; if they are sensible, it is for the saints. Either way, they aren’t serving themselves.

f.g: Out of our minds — perhaps a charge from critics.

chapters.n: Christ’s love drives them. Since one died for all, all had died — Christ represented everyone.

f.w: the love of Christ constraineth us

chapters.n: He died for all so that those who live would no longer live for themselves but for Him who died and rose for them.
So they no longer evaluate anyone by worldly standards. Paul once misjudged Christ that way, but no longer.

f.g: From a merely human point of view.

chapters.n: Anyone in Christ is a new creation. The old life is gone; everything has become new.
All this comes from God, who restored our relationship with Him through Christ and gave the apostles the ministry of reconciliation.
God was in Christ, reconciling the world to Himself, not counting people’s sins against them, and entrusting the apostles with this message.

f.g: Not charging their sins to their account.

chapters.n: The apostles are Christ’s ambassadors; God pleads through them. In Christ’s place they urge: be reconciled to God!

f.g: Official envoys speaking with their sovereign’s authority.

chapters.n: God made the sinless Christ to bear our sin, so that in Him we might become righteous. This is the great exchange of the Atonement.

f.w: made him to be sin for us

chapters.n: As God’s co-workers, the apostles plead with the saints not to receive God’s grace and then let it go to waste.
Quoting Isaiah, Paul declares that the favorable time God promised is here. Now is the day of salvation — don’t delay.

f.w: I have heard thee in a time accepted
now is the day of salvation

chapters.n: They try not to put any obstacle in anyone’s way, so their ministry won’t be discredited.
Instead they prove themselves true servants of God through great endurance in trouble, hardship, and distress.
They endure beatings, imprisonments, riots, exhausting work, sleepless nights, and hunger.
They commend themselves by purity, understanding, patience, kindness, the Holy Ghost, and sincere love.
By truthful speech, God’s power, and righteousness as weapons in both hands — for attack and defense.

f.w: armour of righteousness on the right hand and on the left
f.g: A sword in one hand, a shield in the other.

chapters.n: Through honor and dishonor, slander and praise. They are called deceivers, yet they speak the truth.
Ignored, yet known to God; always near death, yet alive; punished, yet not killed.
Sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; poor, yet making many rich; owning nothing, yet possessing everything. These paradoxes describe true discipleship.

f.w: having nothing, and yet possessing all things

chapters.n: Paul speaks with complete openness and his heart is wide open to them.
There’s no lack of room for them in Paul’s heart; the restriction is in their own affections toward him.

f.g: In the KJV, the seat of tender feelings — affections.

chapters.n: Speaking as a father to his children, he asks them to open their hearts to him in return.
Paul warns against binding partnerships with unbelievers that compromise faith — like yoking two very different animals to one plow. Light and darkness don’t mix.
What harmony does Christ have with Belial, a name for Satan? What does a believer share with an unbeliever in the deepest matters?

f.g: Hebrew for “worthlessness”; used as a name for Satan.

chapters.n: God’s temple has nothing in common with idols. The saints are God’s living temple, as He promised: I will dwell among them and be their God.

f.w: ye are the temple of the living God

chapters.n: So, as Isaiah said, come out and be separate; don’t touch what is unclean, and the Lord will welcome you.

f.w: come out from among them, and be ye separate

chapters.n: God promises to be a Father to them; they will be His sons and daughters — a family relationship, not mere rule-keeping.

f.w: ye shall be my sons and daughters

chapters.n: With God’s promises to be their Father in view, Paul urges the saints to cleanse themselves of everything that defiles body and spirit, becoming fully holy out of reverence for God.
Paul asks them to make room for him in their hearts. He has wronged, corrupted, or cheated no one.

f.g: Make room for us (in your hearts).

chapters.n: He doesn’t say this to condemn them; they are so dear to him that he would live or die with them.

f.w: to die and live with you

chapters.n: Paul speaks boldly and boasts of them. Even amid trouble, he overflows with comfort and joy.

f.w: exceeding joyful in all our tribulation

chapters.n: Resuming his travel story from chapter 2: in Macedonia he had no rest — conflicts outside and fears within.

f.w: when we were come into Macedonia

chapters.n: But God, who comforts the downcast, comforted him through Titus’s arrival.

f.w: comforteth those that are cast down

chapters.n: Even more comforting was Titus’s report: the Corinthians longed to see Paul, grieved over the problems, and were zealous for him.

f.g: Their sorrow over what had happened.

chapters.n: Paul’s severe letter hurt them. He had briefly regretted sending it, but no longer does, since the sorrow was short-lived.
He rejoices — not that they were hurt, but that their sorrow led them to repent. Their grief was the kind God wants.
Godly sorrow leads to repentance and salvation, with no regrets. Worldly sorrow — just feeling bad, or sorry about consequences — leads to death.

f.g: Regret over being caught or suffering, without a changed heart.

chapters.n: Look at what godly sorrow produced in them: earnestness, eagerness to set things right, indignation at sin, reverent fear, longing, zeal, and readiness to see justice done.

f.g: Here, readiness to see wrong punished — justice.

chapters.n: Paul wrote not mainly for the offender or the one offended, but so the saints would see how much they really care for him before God.

f.w: his cause that had done the wrong

chapters.n: Paul is comforted, and he rejoices even more at Titus’s joy — they had refreshed his spirit.
Paul had boasted to Titus about the Corinthians, and they didn’t let him down. His boasting proved true.
Titus’s affection for them grows as he remembers their obedience and the respectful way they received him.
Paul rejoices that he can have complete confidence in them.
Paul turns to the collection for the poor in Jerusalem. He wants the Corinthians to know how God’s grace has worked among the churches of Macedonia.
Though severely tested and extremely poor, the Macedonians’ overflowing joy produced amazing generosity.
Paul testifies they gave as much as they could — even more — and did so voluntarily.
They begged Paul for the privilege of sharing in this service to the saints.
They exceeded expectations because first they gave themselves to the Lord, and then to the apostles’ direction.

f.w: first gave their own selves to the Lord

chapters.n: So Paul asked Titus, who had started this work in Corinth, to help them complete their gift.
The Corinthians excel in faith, speech, knowledge, diligence, and love — they should excel in generosity too.

f.g: Excel in the gift of giving as well.

chapters.n: Paul isn’t commanding; he’s using others’ eagerness to test how genuine their love is.
The ultimate example: Jesus, though rich in heavenly glory, became poor for our sakes so that we could become rich through His poverty.

f.w: though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor

chapters.n: Paul advises them to finish what they eagerly started a year ago — they were the first to want to give.
Now finish it, so their willingness is matched by doing, according to their means.

f.w: out of that which ye have
f.g: From what they own — no more is expected.

chapters.n: If the willing heart is there, the gift is accepted based on what a person has, not on what he doesn’t have.
Paul doesn’t want others relieved while the Corinthians are burdened.
It’s about fairness: their abundance meets others’ needs now, and one day others may help them. The goal is equality.
Paul recalls the manna: those who gathered much had no excess, and those who gathered little had enough.

f.w: He that had gathered much had nothing over

chapters.n: Paul thanks God for giving Titus the same deep care for them.
Titus welcomed Paul’s request, but he was eager to go to them on his own initiative anyway.
With Titus Paul sends a brother widely praised among the churches for his gospel service. His name isn’t given.

f.g: Unnamed; some have guessed Luke, but no one knows.

chapters.n: This brother was chosen by the churches to travel with Paul with the gift, for the Lord’s glory and to show their eagerness to help.
Paul wanted no one to accuse him of mishandling this large sum.

f.w: that no man should blame us

chapters.n: He aims to be honest not only before the Lord but also visibly before people.
He also sends another brother, often proven diligent, who is especially eager because he trusts the Corinthians.
Titus is Paul’s partner; the other brothers are representatives of the churches and bring honor to Christ.

f.g: Greek apostoloi — envoys sent by congregations.

chapters.n: So show these men, and through them all the churches, the proof of your love and that Paul’s boasting about you was justified.
Paul says he really doesn’t need to write about the relief collection — they already know about it.
He has boasted to the Macedonians that Achaia (Corinth’s province) was ready a year ago, and their zeal inspired many.

f.g: Stirred up, motivated (in a good sense).

chapters.n: He is sending the brethren ahead so his boasting about them won’t prove empty.
If Macedonians came with Paul and found them unprepared, Paul — not to mention the Corinthians — would be embarrassed.
So the brethren will arrange the promised gift in advance, so it is a generous gift and not something squeezed out of them.

f.g: Here, a grudging gift given under pressure.

chapters.n: A farmer who plants few seeds reaps a small harvest; one who plants generously reaps generously.
Each should give what he decides in his heart — not reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
God can give them more than enough of every blessing, so they have all they need and plenty to share in good works.
Paul quotes a psalm about the righteous person who gives freely to the poor and whose righteousness lasts forever.

f.w: He hath dispersed abroad; he hath given to the poor

chapters.n: God, who gives seed to farmers and bread for food, will multiply their resources and enlarge the harvest of their righteousness.
They will be enriched in every way so they can be generous, and their giving will produce thanksgiving to God.
This service not only meets the saints’ needs but overflows in many prayers of thanks to God.

f.g: The poverty of the Jerusalem saints.

chapters.n: The Jewish saints will praise God for the Gentile Corinthians’ obedience to the gospel and their generous sharing — a bridge between Jewish and Gentile believers.

f.g: Obedience that matched what they professed.

chapters.n: And the Jerusalem saints will pray for them, longing to see them because of God’s abundant grace in their lives.
Paul ends with praise: thanks be to God for His indescribable gift — His Son.

f.g: A gift too great for words.

chapters.n: Chapters 10–13 change tone sharply as Paul confronts rivals in Corinth. He appeals by Christ’s meekness and gentleness, quoting critics who said he was timid in person but bold in letters.

f.w: the meekness and gentleness of Christ

f.g: Humble, lowly — here, critics called him unimpressive.

chapters.n: He begs them not to force him to be bold in person against those who claim he acts from worldly motives.

f.g: Acted by merely human, selfish standards.

chapters.n: Though they live as mortal men, they don’t wage their battles by worldly methods.

f.g: Fight with human weapons and tactics.

chapters.n: Their weapons aren’t physical but have God’s power to demolish fortresses of error.

f.w: the weapons of our warfare are not carnal

f.g: Fortresses — here, strongholds of false reasoning.

chapters.n: They tear down arguments and every proud barrier raised against knowing God, taking every thought captive to obey Christ.
Once the congregation’s obedience is complete, Paul stands ready to discipline any remaining disobedience.
They are judging by surface appearances. If someone is confident he belongs to Christ, he should realize Paul belongs to Christ just as much.
Even if Paul boasted more about his authority — given by the Lord to build them up, not tear them down — he wouldn’t be ashamed.

f.w: for edification, and not for your destruction

chapters.n: He doesn’t want to seem like he’s trying to frighten them with his letters.
Critics said Paul’s letters were impressive and forceful, but in person he was unimpressive and a poor speaker.

f.g: Not worth listening to — he lacked trained rhetoric.

chapters.n: Such critics should realize that what Paul says in letters, he will do in person.

f.w: in deed when we are present

chapters.n: Paul refuses to rank himself with those who praise themselves. Measuring themselves by their own standard and comparing among themselves shows a lack of wisdom.
Paul will boast only within the field of work God assigned him — which includes Corinth.

f.g: The territory or sphere marked out for him.

chapters.n: He isn’t overreaching. He was the first to bring the gospel all the way to Corinth.

f.w: we are come as far as to you

chapters.n: He doesn’t take credit for others’ work. He hopes that as their faith grows, his sphere of work will expand through them.
Then he can preach in regions beyond Corinth, rather than boasting about work already done in someone else’s territory.
As Jeremiah taught, if anyone boasts, let him boast in the Lord.

f.w: he that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord

chapters.n: It isn’t the one who praises himself who is approved, but the one the Lord commends.
Paul, uncomfortable with boasting, asks them to put up with a little “foolishness” as he plays the boasting game his rivals play.

f.g: Paul ironically calls his self-defense foolish.

chapters.n: His jealousy over them is God’s kind. Like a father who has promised his daughter in marriage, he wants to present them pure to Christ, their bridegroom.
He fears that as the serpent tricked Eve, their minds might be led away from sincere and pure devotion to Christ.
If someone preaches a different Jesus, a different spirit, or a different gospel, they put up with it all too easily.
Paul considers himself in no way inferior to these “super-apostles.”

f.g: Sarcastic — the self-styled “super-apostles” in Corinth, not the Twelve.

chapters.n: He may be untrained as a speaker, but not in knowledge — and he has made that plain to them in every way.
Was it a crime for Paul to lower himself by preaching to them free of charge? Some saw refusing pay as a sign of being second-rate.
In a sense, he “robbed” other churches by accepting their support so he could serve the Corinthians.

f.g: A deliberately strong word for accepting support.

chapters.n: When he ran short in Corinth, believers from Macedonia supplied his needs. He never burdened the Corinthians and never will.

f.w: the brethren which came from Macedonia

chapters.n: As surely as Christ’s truth is in him, no one in Achaia will stop him from this boast of preaching without pay.
Why? Because he doesn’t love them? God knows he does.

f.g: An appeal to God as witness.

chapters.n: He will keep doing this to deprive his rivals of any chance to claim they work on the same terms he does.
Such men are false apostles — deceitful workers disguised as apostles of Christ.
That’s no surprise: Satan himself disguises himself as an angel of light.

f.w: Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light

chapters.n: So his servants masquerade as servants of righteousness. In the end they will get what their deeds deserve.
Paul repeats: don’t think him a fool. But if they do, let them hear him boast a little.

f.g: Paul plays the role of a fool to make his point.

chapters.n: This boasting isn’t how the Lord would speak; Paul does it “foolishly,” only to answer his rivals.
Since many boast in worldly credentials, Paul will too, for a moment.
With biting irony: they are so wise, they gladly put up with fools!

f.g: You put up with fools gladly.

chapters.n: They tolerate being enslaved, exploited, robbed, looked down on, and even slapped in the face by the false teachers.

f.g: A great insult in that culture.

chapters.n: To his shame, Paul admits he was too “weak” to treat them that way! Yet whatever others dare boast of, he can too.

f.g: Paul keeps reminding them this boasting is a role.

chapters.n: Are his rivals Hebrews, Israelites, Abraham’s descendants? So is Paul.

f.w: Are they Hebrews? so am I

chapters.n: Are they servants of Christ? Paul more so — with harder labor, more beatings, more imprisonments, and frequent brushes with death.
Five times Jewish authorities gave him thirty-nine lashes — the legal maximum minus one, to avoid exceeding the limit.
Three times beaten with Roman rods, once stoned, three times shipwrecked, and once adrift at sea a full day and night.
Constant travel and dangers everywhere: rivers, robbers, his own people, Gentiles, city, wilderness, sea, and false believers.
Exhaustion, pain, sleepless nights, hunger and thirst, frequent fasting, cold, and lack of clothing.
On top of all that, he carries daily concern for all the churches.

f.w: the care of all the churches

chapters.n: When anyone is weak, he feels weak; when anyone is led into sin, he burns with grief and indignation.
If he must boast, he will boast about his weaknesses, which show God’s power.
God the Father of Jesus Christ, forever praised, knows Paul is telling the truth.
In Damascus, the governor under King Aretas guarded the city to arrest him.

f.g: Aretas IV, king of the Nabataeans (around 9 BC–AD 40).

chapters.n: But he was lowered in a basket through a window in the wall and escaped. Paul ends his boast with an undignified retreat — the opposite of a war hero’s honor.

f.w: in a basket was I let down by the wall

chapters.n: Boasting isn’t helpful, but since rivals claimed spiritual experiences, Paul will speak of visions and revelations from the Lord.

f.w: visions and revelations of the Lord

chapters.n: Paul modestly speaks of himself in the third person: fourteen years earlier he was caught up to the “third heaven.” He doesn’t know whether he was in his body or out of it.

f.g: The highest heaven, God’s presence; Latter-day Saints often connect it with the celestial glory.
Paul himself, speaking humbly in the third person.

chapters.n: He repeats that only God knows whether it happened in or out of the body.
He was taken into paradise and heard sacred things that may not be spoken.

f.w: not lawful for a man to utter

chapters.n: He’ll boast about that experience, but about himself he will boast only of his weaknesses.
Boasting of this wouldn’t be foolish since it is true, but he refrains so no one thinks more of him than what they see and hear.
To keep him humble after such revelations, Paul was given a “thorn in the flesh,” a messenger of Satan to torment him. What exactly it was, he never says.

f.g: An unnamed affliction — perhaps illness, poor eyesight, or persecution; scripture doesn’t say.

chapters.n: He pleaded with the Lord three times to take it away — as Jesus prayed three times in Gethsemane.
The Lord answered: “My grace is sufficient for you; my power is made perfect in weakness.” So Paul gladly boasts of weakness, so Christ’s power may rest on him.

f.w: My grace is sufficient for thee

f.g: Literally “tabernacle over me,” like God’s presence over the tabernacle.

chapters.n: So Paul is content with weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and troubles for Christ. When he is weak, then he is strong.

f.w: when I am weak, then am I strong

chapters.n: He has become a “fool” by boasting, but they forced him to. They should have defended him, since he is not inferior to the “super-apostles,” even though he is nothing.
The true marks of an apostle — signs, wonders, and miracles — were done among them with great patience.
How were they shortchanged compared to other churches, except that Paul never burdened them financially? “Forgive me this wrong!” he says ironically.
He is ready for a third visit and still won’t burden them. He wants them, not their money — parents provide for children, not the reverse.

f.w: I seek not yours, but you

chapters.n: He will gladly spend everything, and himself, for their souls — even if loving them more seems to make them love him less.
Paul quotes an accusation: maybe he didn’t take money directly, but he was sly and tricked them some other way.

f.w: being crafty, I caught you with guile
f.g: A charge made by his critics, which Paul repeats in order to answer it.

chapters.n: Did he exploit them through any messenger he sent?

f.g: Take advantage of you for profit.

chapters.n: He sent Titus and another brother. Did Titus take advantage? No — they all acted with the same spirit and integrity.
Paul isn’t defending himself to win their approval; he speaks before God in Christ, all to build them up.
He fears he’ll find them not as he hopes — full of quarreling, jealousy, anger, rivalry, slander, gossip, arrogance, and disorder.
He fears God will humble him among them and he will grieve over many who haven’t repented of sexual sins.
Paul’s third visit is coming. He cites the law’s principle that every charge must be confirmed by two or three witnesses — he will deal with matters fairly.

f.w: In the mouth of two or three witnesses

chapters.n: He warned them on his second visit and warns again now: when he comes, he won’t spare those who continue in sin.
They wanted proof that Christ speaks through Paul. Christ isn’t weak toward them, but powerful among them.

f.w: a proof of Christ speaking in me

chapters.n: Christ was crucified in weakness, yet lives by God’s power. Likewise the apostles are weak in Him but will live with Him by God’s power in dealing with them.

f.w: liveth by the power of God

chapters.n: Rather than testing Paul, they should test themselves: are they living in the faith? Don’t they realize Christ is in them — unless they fail the test?

f.g: Those who fail the test, disqualified.

chapters.n: Paul trusts they’ll see that he hasn’t failed the test.
He prays they will do no wrong — not so he looks good, but so they do what is right, even if he seems to have failed.
The apostles can’t act against the truth, only for it.
He is glad to be weak if they are strong. What he prays for is their full restoration and maturity.

f.g: Being fully restored, mended, made complete.

chapters.n: He writes now so that when he comes, he won’t have to be harsh in using the authority the Lord gave him to build up, not tear down.

f.w: to edification, and not to destruction

chapters.n: His farewell: rejoice, aim for wholeness, take comfort, be united, live in peace — and the God of love and peace will be with them.

f.g: Be made complete, set things right.

chapters.n: Greet one another with a holy kiss of affection.
All the saints with Paul send their greetings.

f.g: The believers in Macedonia, where Paul was writing.

chapters.n: Paul closes with a blessing naming all three members of the Godhead: the grace of Christ, the love of God the Father, and the fellowship of the Holy Ghost.

f.w: the communion of the Holy Ghost
f.g: Fellowship and sharing that the Holy Ghost creates.
